comments.text:
PLZ NOTE: these are very general overviews; otherwise, this top 10 video would be 2 hrs long. All of these brands have different offerings for different purposes, etc. I just snagged a representative from each company. If there is any topic you think we should cover about these in particular, please let me know. All ears. Thanks as always for watching!

Hello everyone! Hope you're all enjoying your day. We did a vid last year on why you're always cold that features a TON more down jackets -- in case you wanted more. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tIMhDEVghPc&t=779s&pp=ygUWd2h5IHlvdSdyZSBhbHdheXMgY29sZA%3D%3D

**Also, for Fjallraven -- we did the Greenland No. 1 before, but I wanted to wax it. If you're looking for a heavier weight winter coat, you can check out this baddie: https://www.fjallraven.com/us/en-us/men/jackets/winter-jackets/expedition-down-lite-jacket-m/ (or anything...idk why I'm telling you this)**

Pooping on Canada Goose has its place now. But during a store closing in Toronto in 2010, I got my Canada Goose for $350 CDN and wear only on very cold days, or the occasional weekend trip. Still in tip top shape, including the original, natural trim. Still can't believe what the same parka costs in 2026.

the decathlon MT900 is 139€ which includes 20% VAT - in most of europe - they really have insane value for money

It is pretty much a Walmart for all sports stuff

You could make video purely on Canadian brands. The canadian fashion industry is ridiculously small. But they have dozens of high quality jacket brands that are sold worldwide. like MooseKnuckles, Makage, Arc'teryx and of course Canada Goose. 

Theres also many smaller brands that punch above their weight when it comes to quality. Most Canadian fashion brands have gone bankrupt as fashion has become globalised. But Canadian winter outerwear is still expanding.

Just food for thought :)

I bought a Eddie Bauer First Ascent mountaineering/expedition jacket/parka (Peak XV maybe) some 15 years ago. I live 100 miles from arctic circle, it's seriously cold here. But oh crap, you can't wear that almost ever. It's a furnace. :D Therefore I prefer my Marmot Guide's Down Jacket most of the time. If I have to stand still in -40°C/F I will choose the Eddie Bauer one.

Canada Goose is made in Winnipeg, where I live. About 30 years ago my dad found Canada Goose jackets at Odd Lots, an overstock seller of leftover products in a somewhat sketchy part of town near the factory, for $50 a pop; so our whole family got Canada Goose jackets for about $230 after tax. My sister and I didn't know the brand, but my dad swore by them. My mom might even still have them around somewhere for the grandkids now. Shortly after that we ended up with Arctic Cat snowmobiling jackets which were a lot less bulky for snowmobiling and being towed behind the snowmobile on a sled (as well as being fluorescent green and neon purple). Good times.
The Decathalon is a winner. Although I did get a baffled Sierra Designs parka for $120 some years ago. No chest pockets but 850 fill.
uniglo ultralight down was the best 59 buck I've ever spent. They wear like iron, fit under a nicer coat if you want to style and are warm AF for where I live.
I bought a Joop! down coat in 2008 for about  $500. Survived very comfortably minus 60 F on a project in Siberia in 2008-2009. I am still wearing it on cold winter days in Ohio.

I've been buying montbell and feathered friends for years now and I love them. The main montbell down jackets are intended as liner jackets, to be worn underneath rain shells or other jackets. They're amazing at this because they have minimal hardware, are super light, and pack down super small. My main one weighs 5.7 oz and stuffs down smaller than a nalgene bottle. I'm a backpacker, so having versatile layers is super important to me. The feathered friends helios and volant jackets are much puffier and warmer but they wont layer beneath another jacket quite as easily. Also, their pillows and comforters are amazing. Taion didn't make it on your list but their Hanten down cardigans are my favorite for around town and for the house.
I’ve had both North face and now Canada Goose. Canada goose is the warmest jacket I’ve ever had. In 0-10 Degree snow

1. Patagonia: 10:04
2. Decathlon: 5:32
3. Montbell: 13:09
4. Fjällräven: 14:09
5. RAB: 12:15
6. Feathered Friends: 15:14
7. North Face: 7:58
8. Uniqlo: 1:57
9. Eddie Bauer: 4:47

Honorable Mentions?
Mountain Hardware: 11:10
Heritage Monsters: 16:18
Wife has had the fjällräven no 1 jacket in oxblood red since 2020. Still basically looks brand new.

I bought my CG Edgewood in 2019. Held up perfectly until last winter, when my cuffs started fraying and the coat started smelling weird. Took it to the boutique, sent it in for repair and dry cleaning. They charged me for dry cleaning (50€, whereas my local guy said 110€ for a down coat this size), repairs free of charge (brand new cuffs and flaps replaced due to discoloring). Express shipped back to my house. All in all 50€ plus taxes. And was also told I have lifelong warranty for the coat. Looks like brand new. Couldn't be happier. You don't get there service with the "cheaper" brands.

My Feathered Friends Rock & Ice only comes out for the real cold, -20C or lower.
I have a down vest and ‘sweater’ from Montbell that I purchased a couple of decades ago. The nylon is superlight though I’m not sure what denier, but no tears yet :  ) I use them mostly for layering though, so not exposed to twigs and such.

I use Patagonia exclusively since if you tear it or whatever, you go to their store and they'll repair it for FREE and mail back to your house a month later. I've done this many times.  Their Repair dept. leaves it like new!  And if they can't fix it, they give you store credit of the value when it was sold.  They're basically unbeatable! I also have an Outlet close by, so the end of Season sales are outstanding!  Plus, they have long sleeves for my tall body and more svelte looking vs the competition.

I also have a Canada Goose down parka which I got on a Summer Super Sale 20 years ago.  I believe I paid $110, shipped from Canada.  That jacket now costs a King's ransom since they exploded in popularity.  I got my jacket when they were still niche and not popular.  I only found out about CG back then b/c I saw  "the making of" a movie on a DVD Extras where all the movie people used them while standing around on a really cold arctic level movie set.  Mine is a totally thick, heavy overbuilt jacket!! LOL!  Old school!  I don't whip it out unless it's extremely cold and helps cover my lower butt. Horses for courses as they say!  I'll be ready when Armageddon hits, that's for sure!

I also own a 15 yr old synthetic Cabelas jacket $250 (bought for $90 end of season).  Waterproof lining.  Warm.  Lots of pockets. Attractive looking. The bees knees! ....It's another brand that is great, besides the usual suspects listed in this video.

👉But come on, Patagonia service and quality and End of Season Outlet pricing?!  They just can't be beat!
You want crazy pricing the MT900 is $180 CDN ( $132 US).

I used a Parka from Canada Goose for something like 8 years, when I replaced it I moved to one from Canadiens as Canada Goose prices went up like crazy. I have to admit that Canadiens is every bit as good as Canada Goose, maybe it even has a better outer fabric, softer but as durable.

Coming from a warm, coastal country, I had never experienced extreme cold. During a trip to Kashmir last winter, I bought a Uniqlo down jacket and layered it with fleece. It performed excellently, was reasonably priced, and met all my expectations.
My wife has a canada goose jacket actually two; one extreme weather and a lighter version.  The biggest problem with them is she has to constantly take off because she is sweating in them.
It's crazy how good (and cheap) Decathlon products are. I have a duffel bag that gets used almost exclusively for check-in and hikes, and it's still holding up.

+1 for Fjallraven. After trying a bunch of different jackets, I'd just rather have the durability. Plus as an added little personal touch I leather dye the Zipper leather red and the shoulder patch black.

Fjällräven really is great. As in, inheriting your grandfathers coat in prime condition. Expensive as fuck, but second/third whatever hand makes it affordable, and since the quality is great, it doesn't matter.

Well, if the internet says....
The only jacket mentioned that makes sense if you REALLY get out there is the MH. If you'd gone with the Rab Microlight that would have made sense too. The others are for warmth just standing around or being seen walking to a coffee shop. Outdoors gear being co-opted by city people has really impacted the industry.

I bought a Canada Goose down parka from a mate who managed to get engine oil all over it. I paid him £150 for it and paid the dry cleaner down the road from me £17 and he got the oil out. I’ve had it for 7 years now and it’s still great!
I wore the Uniqlo one for 5 years everyday during winter. No issues. Still have the jacket and wear every now and then.
I beleive North Face is called a life style brand now.

One attribute I think should be discussed in such reviews is how much a jacket or parka can physically protect you when you hit the ground. Twice I have slipped and fallen on frozen ground in a way that I could have seriously hurt myself, my head crashed on the ice and it happened so fast there was no way I could react. I am not an adventure guy, I am just a 50+ leisure traveler who loves the North, so in theory both my Canada Goose Expedition parka and my Arc'teryx Alpha parka are overkill. But I sure needed their protection when those falls happened, and they delivered. Just a suggestion. Love the videos.

Decathalon is a big brand in Europe.  When I lived in Germany it was probably my favorite store.  They have very reasonably priced gear that is very good quality and value.  It's not quite the same quality as top end brands but the value is insanely good.  You're essentially paying Walmart prices to get NorthFace quality.

Fjallraven Polar Expedition is the warmest. Had mine for 35 years, still in great condition, but even though it is still being sold it is nearly $1,000.00 Canadian. But I wear a short sleeve T shirt under it at 30 below with no problem. And one thing a lot of people don’t know, is that a lot of places use duck down, which is not as good as goose down. Has to do with the natural oil content in the down. Oil results in the down eventually starting to cling together and duck down has more oil in it, but it is cheaper.

I lived in Japan for many years and the cheapest stuff I got on a whim in Japan was always better than expensive, highly-rated stuff in the States. I think there are just higher quality standards amongst the general public (in multiple areas--for example beauty products are significantly better but much cheaper in Japan). I wish the US could get onboard because the knowhow is there.

So the thing about the ultra-light down jackets is that they really have a specific use case--you need weight as low as possible in a really cold environment mainly when you aren't moving much or in rare circumstances.  When I solo trekked to Nepal for three weeks I only wore my Cerium during the day maybe three times--it's main use was after trekking to stay warm in unheated teahouses.  So if you aren't in a situation where every ounce counts to keep you as warm as possible you don't need to spend the extra money on them.
Oh good my favorite winter holiday has come, the "Iron Snail goes way deep on down jackets" video!

i sound biased saying this, cause i love uniqlo, but i think their down jacket is the best bang for your buck. they essentially release the same product every year, "improving" (subjective) on their previous year, and keeping the price the same. best part is that you can buy the jacket on sale at the end of season for anywhere between $100-120, sometimes even less. your wallet won't hurt as much, especially if you accidentally rip/tear/damage it, which is really easy for anyone to do.

life span? longest one i've had is 4 years (i live NJ), hasn't flaked, and i usually rip one the longer i own it cause it's not "new" anymore. i wash it the same way as you would a north face puffer; close all zippers, inside out, delicates cycle; dry on low heat with the dryer balls to get that fluff back. never had a problem. it takes a long time in the dryer, but that's every down jacket

Canadian here. I have a Pajar parka I bought over 12 years ago.  I have been out in minus 30+ degrees Celsius with a light sweat shirt on underneath and did not feel the cold.  Awesome Canadian made jacket.

Best looking on you: #1 Rab #2 Fjallraven #3 Heritage coats.  The shoulder/hip ratio, length (where it hits the hips), and size/shape of the quilt squares made the Rab the best-looking (mens) coat.

The Decathlon also looked good, but I didn't get to see enough of the full-body fit, and it looked lumpy/slumpy in the side pic...but I'm not sure that matters if it gives you most of what you want in a jacket.
Cries in Arc'teryx Thorium
My best down jacket is by Bench. Bought it in around 2016, still in great shape. It comes out on the coldest of days.

Down jackets should not be water proof or even water resistant. You only wear them in sub zero conditions when water comes in the from of ice and snow. If it is cold and rainy you should choose other garments.

As far as warmth goes, goose down was king until the 1980s when it was overtaken by synthetics. The issue with down is that it does not maintain loft, which is how it holds warmth, when wet. So you MUST have not only a  waterproof shell over it, but it must also be breathable, otherwise the moisture from inside is just as bad as from the outside. 

I've been wearing high quality down coats in bitterly cold weather since the 1970s. I now have synthetics that aren't cheap, but they put down to shame when it comes to warmth. I've skied in up to -20 F and been toasty warm in my synthetic parkas on more than one occasion. The one aspect that down wins is in weight, but it absolutely is no longer the warmest type of gear.

Wow those shots in the woods with the sun backlighting through the trees are so cinematic and beautiful. That's some prime filming location, almost too nice for a clothing comparison video lol but you're worth it

I have a montbell 800 down lightweight jacket and think it is really good for autumn, spring, or as a mid layer. Extremely light. I am really impressed with Montbell's quality vs price especially so as it's not trying to be a budget brand. Other brands I see in shops (Mainly Outsiders store in London): CAYL, Snow Peak, Peak Performance, Goldwin

I got a Canada Goose jacket ten years ago and the prices were totally different then, high tho but not as now. It has been one hell of a jacket, still looks brand new after all the abuse I have given it, skiing, ATV driving, walking in forest and working on our ranch with it and sledding with the kids. 
Most folks buy them as show offs but they are actually really really durable and warm. The prices are insane now tho.
The decathlon is 100€ in Germany atm (you can get it even cheaper if you have corporate benefits). Their stuff is good money value in general. Just ordered it for 80€
I suppose the relative advantage of decathlon is that it is definitely not a fashion brand by any stretch of the imagination. The only way it stays competitive is to focus on features and price point

I'm in the cold a lot, and I used to freeze a lot doing my job, until I saved up some money to buy some proper cold weather gear. My blue Patagonia 'ski' fit (which includes the coat you reviewed - I bought it on sale - during the start of a record breaking blizzard...) was a game changer. My Canada Goose (I bought it used) even more-so. It's the long floofy black one. It goes down to my ankles and keeps me warm in the blind where I document gooses... among other things. The lady I bought it from said I'd be too warm in it. The thing is, if you're sitting still documenting gooses (ahem - geese) in a damp blind... you're going to get cold. Lucky for me - I've never been too cold wearing my black floofy.  (I wish I could say the same for the Patagonia - which gives you an idea of how cold I was before the Patagonia...). Sometimes, (on those -40F and colder windchill days) I find myself wearing my Patagonia blue fit under my floofy Canada Goose. I don't know how that effective that is... but hey... I'm warm, so it's cool.

Thanks for your breakdown. Well done!
For the same price the Patagonia’s classic Down Sweater Hoodie has 800 FP down & they’ve upped the amount of down for more warmth.
Decathlon is so freaking good for everything I love my decathlon puffer
Outdoor Vitals new Vantage Alpine Down Jacket is my favorite now. 850fill power with about 200g of down (more than most competitors at the 850 fill power spec). Only $275.
Could you do this for synthetics too? I’m allergic to down and while it’s all contained in jackets I don’t risk it. Would love to see options for those of us who can’t use down

I'd say Columbia was the first Outdoor fashion brand. I have 3 down vests and one Jacket from Eddie Bauer. The first vest was purchased in '93 and the other 2 vests and jacket were purchased in '09. All of them are still in great condition and as warm as the day I bought them. The vest from '93 has a rip in the outer shell and not one feather has ever came out of that one or any of them.

FEATHERED FRIENDS FTW! I"ve used their products:  jackets, down pants, sleeping bags, comforters and pillows for over yrs now. As for jackets, I have an old-school Volant, circa 2000 (more like the current Khumbu or Rock & Ice) , and me and my spouse have Helios jackets and vests since the ? mid-2000's. The Volant is AMAZING. I've used it in the backcountry down to -15*F and been totally comfy. That said, our Helios jackets and vests were from when FF decided to experiment with off-shore manufacturing to compete on price. Overall, we are very happy, but the quality was a small step lower. I see that they now make their Helios garments in Seattle, USA.

It's too bad Fjallraven no longer sells it in North America, but the Keb Touring Down Jacket was one of the best down jackets you can buy. It has two zippered hand pockets beneath the insulation, front chest pocket on the outside, two mesh pockets on the inside for gloves, and an internal security pocket inside the right hand pocket. It has a two way zipper, and also buttons in case you want to do it up but still have some airflow.
0:10 high school kids would save up all their McDonald's money to get a jacket with that little logo on the side 😂

-> I nominate the LL Bean WIND CHALLENGER ski parka. It's sorta like a Montbell Plasma that went through Special Forces training and came out tough with a big skill set.
 1.) woven baffles, NOT sewn-thru. 2.) 650 fill DWR (Down Tech) treated down 3.) helmet compatible and fully adjustable hood.   4.) double layer shell on hood, shoulders and elbow to wrist  5.) pit zips!  6.) 2 way "belay" waterproof front zipper. 7.) 2 inside pockets, 4 outside pockets W/ waterproof zippers  8.) durable stretch fabric shell  9.) bottom hem drawstrings W/ cord locks.  
650 fill down is good for garments that will be compressed IN USE, as in leaning back against the back of a chair lift on a frigid day, etc. Why? B/C 650 fill down will not compress nearly as much aa 850 fill down, thus giving you better COMPRESSED insulation. Hey, it ain't likely going into a stuff sack so "compressibility" is not an issue.  US $370. A bit pricey but well worth it for features and famous LL Bean build quality.

Happy to say that I have the exact same Patagonia downdrit and I couldn't be happier with it. One thing I'd add is the range of motion it allows. I have broad shoulders and long limbs and hate being restrained. The range of movement I have in it is awesome.

Also, the Rab definitely suits you the best imo.
Could you do a comparison of winter coats made in Norway and Sweden? They are supposed to be the very best in the industry.
Incredible to see a mention of All Blues Co. The best store in Leeds.
For me the Canada Goose is the best jacket i have ever own. Bought my expedition parka in 2011 for a 1000€. It is still in very good condition and warm asf. 🤘🏻
man, now I just want to wear a dozen down jackets and fall asleep after drinking a hot chocolate. Thank you.

You should do a full video on Feathered Friends, there's very little content available on any of their jackets. I've been wearing their Rock & Ice parka for the last couple of winters, it looks kind of ridiculous, but it's also very nice to wear and by far the warmest 'big parka' I've ever had, makes the Canada Goose Expedition I had before look and feel like a rain coat! 

A couple of interesting facts about FF jackets are that they are mostly 'filled to order' and often exceed the quoted 900 fill power. Each jacket comes with a 'down tracker tag', put the number into the website and you get the exact fill power and down to feather ratio, my Rock & Ice is filled with 908 fill power Hungarian Goose down with a down/feather ratio of 95/5. I also have a Volant Jacket and that one is 905 fill power at a ratio of 93/7.
Military combat garments like Patagonia Mars & Arc’teryx Leaf would be a cool informative vid

Bought Canada goose citadel parka(?) and it lasted for 3 years, then the goose, well the remains of it, started going out from the jacket despite me being careful with it. I now prefer simpler (and cheaper ones).

While you won’t find them on Madison Avenue or Vail slopes, Carhartt has been the rock steady favorite of every farm and ranch. I have a pair of coveralls that are now 30 years old with original metal zippers. I have several others you mention but if I’m out photographing ducks in a blind or finding a calf out in the blizzard, Carhartts have saved me in -30 with 40 mph winds. Indestructible, comfy with age and life saving.
Fjallraven Singi.  Though, there is a huge difference between the men’s and women’s version (men’s is way warmer), and the zipper is difficult.  Otherwise, durable, amazing and so warm.
That Fjallraven coat looked sick after you waxed it
Why nobody is talking about parajumpers? Very warm, waterproof, high quality and relatively good priced.
I ended up with a women's Patagonia Silent Down. It was mixed in with the men's jackets at the store and it fit perfectly. Plus, no logo on the chest!

7:39 Simond is a mountaneering brand that was aquired by Decathlon, Wed’ze on the other hand is Decathlon’s snow line. To be honest, in my experience not THAT great. Good for the price, but if you’re getting more into snowboarding for example there’s definetly better alternatives. Here in europe at least it’s the “beginner gear” kind of brand, low price but once you start skiing more every year you kind of outgrow it.
I have the Rab Positron Pro, and it's exceptionally warm and can withstand sub freezing temps and winds.  Built very well too
I prefer wearing a light down jacket under a hard shell so I can very easily open the ventilation pockets to cool down if needed.
The decathlon jacket is only €140 in Europe, picked one up based on your review. 👍🏼
The decathlon MT900 sadly is only good till -5°C unless you're active, which doesn't help us people waiting for the bus in -20 or colder Canadian Winters.
You covered Eddie Bauer, what about LL Bean?

Decathlon is simply put the best value in outdoors clothing, period. No other brand provides as much quality for such a low price, specially in Europe where prices are much, much lower, i.e., that down jacket costs 140€ over this side of the pond as base price, often on sale for 99€.

It's crazy because watching your videos gives me the sensation that I'm going on a hike with you in the woods but I inexplicably stop at random points which forces you to turn around in order to continue justifying your strange obsession about outdoor clothing wear.
The Rab Mythic G Down jacket imo is their warmest per weight and more comparable to the Montbell 1000. There's a Swedish brand Stellar equipment that makes some super nice down jackets as well.

I remember when Canada Goose wasn't a Lifestyle Brand and offered excellent performance for a good (tho still not cheap) price. It's now almost double the price. I refuse to reward companies for ripping me off. Same goes for Arcteryx.

I found new “trappers” down filled jackets that were made in Manitoba, Canada at an outlet store; likely make in the 1980s.  Mine has a coyote trimmed hood, my wife’s is black-fox.  Paid $100 for each one… we’ve had them 18 years. 
Also, I’d get OSC brand before Canada Goose now days. Canada Goose is for people from Toronto or Vancouver…

Proud owner of a Fjallraven Greenland jacket. Can confirm it is fantastically warm and durable. It not being waterproof can be a downside, but is rarely an issue since it's a serious winter jacket and snow mostly rolls off it.

LoL, interior Alaska here and I've lived without heat in negative 20 temps, it regularly gets below negative 40 here and I don't know anyone in my town with a Canada Goose jacket. Layering is key, not expensive stuff. 

To accompany this video you should make a winter boots comparison video, hint, Bunny boots.
I remember a military surplus company that I follow bought a bunch of the us antarctic Explorer Canadian goose jackets and were like half the new price and had the cool patch.
Absolutely love my EB Superior but a Nobis I picked up recently is now my go to. Have you tried anything from the brand?
Could you please list them according to quality, not price low to high. It‘s confusing.

Does Marmot no longer exist? I am over 70 at this point, so not buying much new cold weather gear. But I have Marmot synthetic down (still works if it gets wet) jackets that I bought back in the day. Thirty or forty years old, has a few patches, but still keeps me warm.
I went for the Eddie Bauer bomber  and the EB Xv with the 800 fill power  it’s hilarious because I have to wait for extreme cold weather to use it and It’s amazing.

Canada Goose has practical high quality models and dumb designer garbage for Toronto posers. I purchased 3 of their expedition jackets (2 coats in one) for myself, my wife and son 10-15 years ago and they are still the best, warmest and most practical 3 season coats we’ve ever owned. The $1300 each price tags amortized over the years of service makes them a fantastic value and worth every penny. Cheers.

Cost per wear and value for money hands down it's the Patagonia Down Sweater/jacket.  Lifetime guarantee with free repairs and on average the clothing will last 20+ years if taken care of properly.  No other clothing brand comes close.  I have clothing from Patagonia thats older than my college age niece's and nephews.

I have a Fjallraven Skogso down jacket thats my go-to cold weather jacket.  Its warm, big, and had an absolute gob of pockets, plus it's indestructible.  One day I really want one of the ones that has a fur lined hood... but I love G1000, it's insanely durable.  I've had the jacket for six years, I suspect Ill have it for the rest of my life.

In my opinion you missed the best down jacket and that's the Pj's (Para jumpers) jacket for extreme cold temperatures my Pj's cost around €600 about 15 years ago and it looks as good now as it did 15 years ago. I live in Finland where I have lived as far north as Levi about 150km above the arctic circle, I've experienced winters as cold as - 45 degrees in the north of Finland to - 35 in the south of Finland. The only thing I've found wrong with the Pj's jacket is that between 0 and - 10 degrees the Pj's is just to warm to wear it works best between - 10 to - 45 or below. It's not the type of jacket you can wear  for instance as an everyday winter jacket as driving in your car after a while or going from shop to shop it's just too warm you end up carrying it in your arm which can be annoying, however if you live and work in extreme conditions, anywhere above the arctic circle, the poles or Siberia I would highly recommend the Pj's it's perfect for military or police who operate in extreme conditions. But to be 100% honest for winters like the ones similar to your video where you could be outside without a wooly hat or gloves on, that doesn't need to be resistant to arctic winds any jacket you previewed would be good for snowball fights, taking your poodle for a walk, that type of thing. But if any of your viewers who may live in Alaska, northern Canada, Lapland or Siberia or works in the north or south pole on station I would highly recommend a Pj's for everything else the jackets you previewed would be fine.
That red Karakoram 😍

I found an Eddie Bauer down jacket made by their pattern department, very well sewn and in excellent condition. No labels except one tag at the top with the style and date of manufacture. I like the uniqueness of it. Are pattern department items of any real value?
Decathlon is absolutely goated. Any kind of gear you need to get into a sport, more adventurous tourism or just everyday life for cheap.
My Eddie Bauer Superior is bulletproof and by far the best value for the money.
I have the rab jacket. I got it for trips to the north of Sweden and I absolutely love it!
I really like my Mackage Edward Fur Parka, albeit the zipper teeth are a little sharp. Super warm 800 fill power with a tougher outer shell
Wait you have decathlon in america too? Thats a legendary brand here in france lol (the streets still remember the dark blue and orange quechua jackets)

Hmm for those that need them sure but down jackets are the pinnacle lifestyles products. They are made of Poly and nylon clingfilm and mostly they sit in closets after people find them too hot for the commute.

Best tip: Buy the jacket used! You can easily find jacket’s in perfect condition for much less than they are brand new, And from good brands as well. I saved about 70% of the price of my jacket by buying it used.

Hmmm...sounds like Canada Goose got a bad shake here just because its gotten expensive-ish compared to the others (but not Moncler) - but even their website says Luxury performance = not cheap. Love my Canada Goose Expedition...so so so warm.
Hi. French here. We can buy the MT900 for around 140€ here.

Feel like you missed a ton of points, and went way ADD.  Also eash jacket here served totally different purposes...  Was looking for an alternative for my CG Wyndam, to wear every day.   So while doing  good job on pooping on the Canada goose, and not explaining any features...  I was left more confused...

Here in Edmonton Alberta, we have weather ranging from -40 to +30 Celsius (I think records go down to -50) 

Regardless, I went for 2 Fjällräven jackets. Their Greenland, and their parka. Best money I’ve spend on winter gear. Durable, long lasting, excellent build, stylish. I would happily take a couple Canada goose, but I prefer the durability of the waxed fabric as I take a more buy it for life approach with my things.
I need this level of analysis for bottoms (all layers) ! The upper body gets too much attention! What are some of the best insulated or fleece-lined pants, thermal long johns, etc.!
Hello from Kittery! Just happened across your channel and it’s been enjoyable. We seem to make very similar choices.

Interested how the Woolrich arctic parka would rank compared to these jackets.

A few words on Decathlon as a guy from Europe:

It's one of the largest retailers (I believe 3rd) and have stores in almost every major city and mountain resort. 

What makes them so competative is their scale and target. They are not going for the serious mountaineers, for example, but for the people who aspire to be, while using their gear to go shopping when it's raining. This is a huge market, especially, if you add the people with kids. The cheap Decathlon for kids is just everywhere, because you don't need it to last more than a year.

So, they have this huge market share and scale, and they can afford enough R&D to stay competative. The truth is that they put a lot of "extras" in their products to convince the customers, that it's a serious gear, although the quality is not great. The lowest end products are great for their price, but if you go to the mid or high tier, it quickly loses value. For example, their "merino" base layers, keep odors like crazy, and they are like 10% cheaper than the other brands.

You can find a lot of gems in Decathlon, but not in every category.

BTW, the US prices are insane - the MT900 is $150 in Europe with taxes and everything.

The jackets picked to review were apples and oranges and a number of them fall into the category of urban street wear. I've worn a lot of different down jackets over the last 50 years and the one I've owned the longest and am happiest with is the FF Volant.  I bought mine, off of eBay for shoulder season mountaineering in the Cascades when I know temps will be sufficiently low that it won't rain.  I wore it this morning with just a wool base layer underneath, inca breezy mid-teens F to walk the dog, and was totally comfortable.  It can be too warm if you are on the move in temperatures above the low/mid-20's F.  It was designed as a belay jacket (you put it on while stopped when climbing or mountaineering) and has minimal features, including the simplest elasticized cuffs.  If you were looking for something to wear around town, you might want butt coverage, which this does not have.  Also, you will definitely look like the staypuff marshmallow man when you wear it.
